content: The transfer of antiretroviral drugs (ARVs), particularly efavirenz (EFV) and tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), through breast milk and their potential effects on neurodevelopmental outcomes, nutritional status (including micronutrient levels), bone metabolism, and growth in infants remain incompletely understood. Pharmacological studies are needed to determine the breast milk-to-maternal plasma drug concentration ratios, as well as infant plasma drug levels, to better understand the drug levels in breast milk and the effective dose delivered to the infant for many ARV drugs currently in use. These data are essential for each ARV drug, as their pharmacokinetic characteristics likely vary between different drugs. Further research is required to elucidate the relationship between maternal viral load and the risk of postnatal HIV transmission, particularly in the context of whether the mother is receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART). Additionally, studies are needed to identify interventions that improve retention in care and adherence to postnatal ARV regimens and breastfeeding practices. Clinical assessment and laboratory testing are critical for evaluating individuals following an HIV diagnosis. These assessments help identify co-infections, noncommunicable diseases (NCDs), and other comorbidities that may influence treatment response. Limited laboratory testing is also recommended to monitor treatment response and detect potential ARV drug toxicities. Laboratory tests for HIV screening and monitoring, as well as for screening co-infections and NCDs, are outlined in clinical guidelines. For HIV diagnosis, recommended tests include HIV serology for adults and children aged 18 months or older, and early infant diagnosis (EID) for children younger than 18 months. Additional tests include CD4 cell count, tuberculosis (TB) symptom screening, hepatitis B virus (HBV) surface antigen (HBsAg) serology, hepatitis C virus (HCV) serology, and cryptococcal antigen testing for individuals with CD4 counts ≤100 cells/mm³. Screening for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and pregnancy testing is also recommended, particularly to prioritize ART initiation in pregnant women to prevent HIV transmission to the child. Assessment for major NCDs and comorbidities is also advised. Before initiating ART, laboratory tests such as hemoglobin levels (for starting zidovudine [AZT]), serum creatinine and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) (for starting TDF), alanine aminotransferase (ALT) (for starting nevirapine [NVP]), and baseline CD4 cell count are recommended. Blood pressure measurement and pregnancy testing are also advised, especially for women of childbearing age not using family planning and receiving dolutegravir (DTG) or low-dose EFV. During ART, routine monitoring includes HIV viral load testing at 6 months, 12 months, and annually thereafter to assess treatment efficacy. CD4 cell count monitoring every 6 months is recommended until patients are stable on ART. Serum creatinine and eGFR should be monitored for individuals on TDF, particularly those at high risk of adverse events, such as those with underlying renal disease, older age, low body mass index (BMI), diabetes, hypertension, or concurrent use of nephrotoxic drugs. For suspected treatment failure, viral load testing is the preferred method to diagnose and confirm treatment failure. If viral load testing is unavailable, CD4 count and clinical monitoring should be used, with targeted viral load testing to confirm failure where possible. Viral failure is defined as a persistently detectable viral load exceeding 1,000 copies/mL based on two consecutive measurements within a 3-month interval, with adherence support provided between tests. Plasma specimens are preferred for viral load testing, but dried blood spot specimens may be used in settings with logistical or operational barriers. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends a viral load threshold of 1,000 copies/mL to define treatment failure, as the risk of HIV transmission and disease progression is very low below this threshold. Viral blips or intermittent low-level viremia (50–1,000 copies/mL) during effective treatment are not associated with an increased risk of treatment failure. Clinical failure is defined as the occurrence of new or recurrent clinical events indicating severe immunodeficiency (WHO clinical stage 4 conditions) after 6 months of effective treatment. Immunological failure is defined as a CD4 count ≤250 cells/mm³ following clinical failure or persistent CD4 levels below 100 cells/mm³ in adults and adolescents. For children, immunological failure is defined as persistent CD4 levels below 200 cells/mm³ for those younger than 5 years or below 100 cells/mm³ for those older than 5 years. In settings where viral load monitoring is unavailable, clinical and CD4 monitoring are recommended, although these criteria have poor sensitivity and specificity for detecting treatment failure, particularly at higher CD4 counts. Alternative approaches, such as single CD4 count thresholds or CD4-based risk charts, have been proposed and merit further validation.
